items.passage: Before each patrol, every crew member inspects the personal flotation device assigned to them. Begin by checking the fabric for tears, fading, or mildew, since damaged material can let the flotation foam absorb water. Next, pull firmly on every strap and buckle to confirm that the stitching holds and the hardware latches. Then squeeze the foam panels; they should spring back rather than stay compressed. Finally, read the label to confirm the device is approved for the wearer's weight range and the type of operation. A device that fails any one of these checks is tagged out of service and turned in to the supply petty officer. Do not attempt a field repair, because a patched jacket cannot be trusted to perform in cold water.
items.stem: According to the passage, what should a crew member do immediately after pulling on the straps and buckles?
choices: Squeeze the foam panels to see if they spring back
Read the label to check the approved weight range
Check the fabric for tears, fading, or mildew
Tag the device out of service and turn it in
items.explanation: The passage gives the steps in order with the words Begin, Next, Then, and Finally. The sentence that starts with Then, right after the strap check, says to squeeze the foam panels. Reading the label comes last, checking the fabric comes first, and tagging out happens only if a check fails.

items.stem: According to the passage, what should be done with a flotation device whose buckle will not latch?
choices: Repair it in the field before the patrol begins
Keep wearing it until a replacement arrives
Tag it out of service and turn it in to the supply petty officer
Test it in cold water to see whether it still floats
items.explanation: The passage states that a device that fails any one of the checks is tagged out of service and turned in to the supply petty officer. The next sentence rules out a field repair, and nothing in the passage allows continued use or a water test.

items.passage: Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun. Most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides in a period slightly longer than a day. When the sun and moon line up with Earth, near a new or full moon, their pulls combine and the tidal range is greatest; these are called spring tides, though they have nothing to do with the season. When the sun and moon are at right angles to each other, their pulls partly cancel and the range is smallest; these are neap tides. Mariners consult tide tables because the depth of water over a sandbar or under a bridge can change by several feet within hours.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Spring tides happen only during the spring season
The sun has no measurable effect on ocean tides
Mariners should avoid sandbars and bridges at all times
Tides are caused by the pull of the moon and sun, and their size depends on how those bodies line up
items.explanation: The first sentence names the cause of tides, and the middle sentences explain that the range is largest when the sun and moon line up and smallest when they are at right angles. Choice A is contradicted by the statement that spring tides have nothing to do with the season, choice B is contradicted by the first sentence, and choice C is a detail stretched into advice the passage never gives.

items.stem: As used in the passage, the word range most nearly means
choices: a stove used for cooking
the difference between high and low water levels
a line of hills or mountains
the distance a vessel can travel on its fuel
items.explanation: The passage says the tidal range is greatest when the pulls combine and smallest when they partly cancel, and it is talking about how far the sea level rises and falls. So range here means the span between high and low water. The other meanings are real uses of the word but do not fit a sentence about tides.

items.passage: Cold water removes heat from the body far faster than cold air at the same temperature. A person who falls overboard in water below about 60 degrees Fahrenheit can lose the use of their hands within minutes, long before the body's core temperature drops to a dangerous level. For this reason, survival instructors teach that the first task after an unexpected immersion is not to swim but to control breathing and get a grip on anything that floats. Swimming toward a distant shore burns energy and pumps warm blood out to the limbs, where the water cools it. A person wearing a flotation device who stays still and keeps their head above the surface will usually last much longer than a strong swimmer who sets out for land.
items.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
choices: Cold air is more dangerous to a person than cold water at the same temperature
Loss of hand function is the only serious effect of cold water on the body
Swimming hard is the best way to keep the body warm after falling overboard
A poor swimmer wearing a flotation device may outlast an expert swimmer who has none
items.explanation: The last sentence says a person with a flotation device who stays still will usually last much longer than a strong swimmer who sets out for land, which supports choice D even though the passage never says it directly. Choice A reverses the first sentence, choice C is contradicted by the sentence about swimming pumping warm blood to the limbs, and choice B ignores the mention of core temperature.

items.passage: For centuries, lighthouses warned ships away from rocks with open fires and later with oil lamps backed by mirrors. These early lights were dim, and much of their glow was wasted by shining upward or into the ground. In the 1820s a French physicist, Augustin Fresnel, designed a lens built from many concentric rings of glass. Each ring bent the light from a single lamp into a flat, horizontal beam, so nearly all of the lamp's output traveled out toward the sea. The lenses were also much lighter than a solid glass lens of the same size would have been. Within a few decades the design had been adopted around the world, and sailors could see a lighthouse from far greater distances than before.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
choices: How a New Lens Made Lighthouses Brighter
The Complete History of Ocean Navigation
The Early Life of Augustin Fresnel
Why Oil Lamps Replaced Open Fires
items.explanation: Every sentence builds toward the lens design and its effect: the beam was focused toward the sea and sailors could see lighthouses from greater distances. Choice B is far too broad, choice C is about a subject the passage never covers, and choice D focuses on a minor detail from the first sentence.

items.passage: Any time a technician services a pump, compressor, or other powered machine, the energy source must be isolated first. Switch off the machine at its own controls, then open the disconnect or breaker that feeds it. Place a personal lock on the disconnect and attach a tag that shows your name and the date. Before touching any moving part, press the start button to confirm the machine does not respond; this test is the only sure proof that the correct circuit was opened. Keep the key to your lock on your person during the entire job. Only the technician who applied a lock may remove it, and it comes off only after tools are cleared and guards are back in place.
items.stem: According to the passage, when should the technician press the start button?
choices: Before opening the disconnect or breaker
After the lock and tag are in place but before touching any moving part
After the job is finished and the guards are back in place
Only if the tag has been removed by someone else
items.explanation: The passage lists the steps in order: switch off, open the disconnect, place the lock and tag, and then, before touching any moving part, press the start button to confirm the machine does not respond. Pressing it before the disconnect is opened would start the machine, and the passage never mentions testing after the job or in response to a missing tag.

items.stem: The author's main purpose in this passage is to
choices: explain how pumps and compressors generate pressure
persuade readers to buy higher quality padlocks
give step-by-step safety instructions for isolating a machine before service
describe the history of workplace safety regulations
items.explanation: The passage is a series of commands: switch off, open, place a lock, press the start button, keep the key. That is the form of a procedure, and the first sentence states its goal, isolating the energy source before service. The passage says nothing about how machines work, about buying locks, or about history.

items.passage: Most substances become denser as they freeze, because their molecules pack closer together in a solid. Water is an unusual exception. As liquid water cools below about 39 degrees Fahrenheit, its molecules begin arranging themselves into an open, six-sided pattern held together by hydrogen bonds. This pattern takes up more room than the loose arrangement in the liquid, so ice ends up less dense than the water around it and floats. The effect matters far beyond a glass of lemonade. Because ice forms a floating layer on lakes and seas, it insulates the water beneath, allowing fish and other organisms to survive the winter. If ice sank, bodies of water would freeze from the bottom up and many would become solid.
items.stem: According to the passage, ice floats because
choices: its molecules form an open pattern that takes up more room than liquid water
hydrogen bonds make frozen water heavier than liquid water
it is warmer than the water that surrounds it
it traps air bubbles as it freezes
items.explanation: The passage says the molecules arrange into an open, six-sided pattern that takes up more room than the loose arrangement in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats. Choice B gets the effect backward, and choices C and D describe causes the passage never mentions.

items.passage: A distress call on marine VHF radio follows a fixed pattern so that any listener can understand it, even when reception is poor. Set the radio to channel 16, the international hailing and distress channel, and turn the power to high. Press the transmit key, say the word Mayday three times, then give the name of the vessel three times. Release the key for a moment, then transmit again with the vessel's position, the nature of the emergency, the number of people aboard, and a description of the boat. End with the word Over and release the key so that a station can reply. If no one answers within a short time, repeat the entire call. Never use the Mayday call for a situation that does not involve grave and immediate danger to life or vessel.
items.stem: After saying Mayday three times and the vessel's name three times, the operator should next
choices: switch the radio to a different channel and wait for a reply
say the word Over and release the key
describe the boat before giving its position
release the key briefly, then transmit the position and nature of the emergency
items.explanation: The passage says to release the key for a moment, then transmit again with the vessel's position, the nature of the emergency, the number of people aboard, and a description of the boat. Over comes at the end, the channel is never changed, and the description of the boat is listed after the position, not before it.

items.passage: The United States Coast Guard traces its roots to 1790, when Congress authorized a small fleet of cutters to enforce customs laws and collect tariffs at the nation's ports. This Revenue Cutter Service operated under the Treasury Department, since import duties were then the federal government's main source of income. A separate organization, the Life-Saving Service, grew up along the coasts during the nineteenth century, staffing stations with crews who rowed surfboats out to wrecked ships. In 1915 the two services were combined under a new name, the Coast Guard. The Lighthouse Service was folded in as well in 1939. Today the service carries out missions as varied as search and rescue, drug interdiction, icebreaking, and the inspection of commercial vessels.
items.stem: According to the passage, the Revenue Cutter Service operated under the Treasury Department because
choices: the Navy had not yet been established
the Treasury was responsible for the nation's lighthouses
import duties were the federal government's main source of income
rescue work along the coast required federal funding
items.explanation: The second sentence states that the service operated under the Treasury Department since import duties were then the federal government's main source of income. The passage never mentions the Navy, lighthouses were a separate service until 1939, and the rescue work belonged to the Life-Saving Service.

items.stem: The passage implies that the original purpose of the cutters authorized in 1790 was primarily to
choices: fight battles against foreign navies
protect government revenue rather than to save lives
maintain lighthouses along the coast
break ice in northern harbors
items.explanation: The first two sentences say the cutters were authorized to enforce customs laws and collect tariffs, and that the service was placed under the Treasury because of import duties. Lifesaving is described as the job of a separate organization, so the cutters' original role was financial and law enforcement. Icebreaking and lighthouses are mentioned only as later additions, and naval combat is never mentioned.

items.passage: Back injuries are among the most common workplace injuries, and most of them happen during ordinary lifting rather than dramatic accidents. The safest lift starts before the object leaves the ground. Size up the load, clear the path you will walk, and get help if the item is bulky or heavier than you can handle comfortably. Stand close to the load with your feet about shoulder width apart, bend at the knees and hips, and keep your back straight as you grip the object. Lift smoothly by straightening your legs, holding the load close to your body. Turn by moving your feet, not by twisting at the waist. Set the load down the same way, bending the knees rather than the back.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Planning the lift and using proper technique prevents common back injuries
Most back injuries are caused by dramatic workplace accidents
Workers should never lift a heavy object without help
Standing with the feet shoulder width apart is the key to safe lifting
items.explanation: The opening sentences say back injuries usually come from ordinary lifting and that a safe lift starts before the object leaves the ground, and the rest of the passage describes the technique. Choice C is too absolute, since help is advised only for bulky or heavy items. Choice B is contradicted by the first sentence, and choice D is one small detail, not the whole idea.

items.passage: Air has weight, and the pressure it exerts on the ground changes as weather systems move through. A barometer measures that pressure. For sailors and pilots, the direction of the change matters more than the number itself. A steady or slowly rising barometer usually signals fair, settled weather, because sinking air in a high-pressure system discourages clouds from forming. A falling barometer warns that a low-pressure system is approaching, bringing rising air, clouds, and often rain or wind. The faster the drop, the stronger the coming weather is likely to be. Experienced mariners log the reading every few hours so that a trend becomes visible long before the sky changes.
items.stem: As used in the passage, the word settled most nearly means
choices: decided by mutual agreement
paid in full
moved to a new location
calm and stable
items.explanation: The passage pairs settled with fair weather and explains that sinking air discourages clouds from forming, so the word describes weather that is calm and not changing. The other choices are real meanings of settled, but none makes sense when describing the weather.

items.passage: Air has weight, and the pressure it exerts on the ground changes as weather systems move through. A barometer measures that pressure. For sailors and pilots, the direction of the change matters more than the number itself. A steady or slowly rising barometer usually signals fair, settled weather, because sinking air in a high-pressure system discourages clouds from forming. A falling barometer warns that a low-pressure system is approaching, bringing rising air, clouds, and often rain or wind. The faster the drop, the stronger the coming weather is likely to be. Experienced mariners log the reading every few hours so that a trend becomes visible long before the sky changes.
items.stem: Based on the passage, a mariner who sees the barometer dropping quickly should expect
choices: clear skies within a few hours
strong wind or rain in the near future
a high-pressure system to arrive
no change in the weather
items.explanation: The passage says a falling barometer warns that a low-pressure system is approaching with clouds and often rain or wind, and that the faster the drop, the stronger the coming weather is likely to be. Clear skies and high pressure go with a rising barometer, not a falling one.

items.passage: Many people believe that the distress signal SOS stands for Save Our Ship or Save Our Souls. In fact the letters were chosen for a simpler reason. In the early days of wireless telegraphy, operators sent messages in Morse code, a system of short and long pulses. Different countries used different distress signals, which caused confusion at sea. An international agreement that took effect in 1908 settled on a single pattern of three short pulses, three long pulses, and three short pulses. That pattern is easy to send, easy to recognize through static, and hard to confuse with ordinary traffic. Written out in letters it happens to spell SOS, and the phrases people attach to it were invented afterward as memory aids.
items.stem: The author's primary purpose in this passage is to
choices: teach the reader how to send messages in Morse code
argue that all ships should be required to carry radios
correct a common misunderstanding about the origin of SOS
describe a famous shipwreck in the early twentieth century
items.explanation: The passage opens with what many people believe and then says in fact the letters were chosen for a simpler reason, which is the pattern of a correction. The final sentence drives the point home by saying the phrases were invented afterward. Morse code is mentioned only as background, and no shipwreck or argument about radios appears.

items.passage: Every container of a hazardous chemical in the shop must carry a label that identifies the product and warns of its dangers. The label uses a set of standard pictograms: a flame for flammable materials, a skull and crossbones for substances that are acutely toxic, and a corroded hand and metal bar for chemicals that can burn skin or eat through metal. Below the pictograms, a signal word tells the reader how serious the hazard is. The word Danger is reserved for the more severe hazards, while Warning marks the less severe ones. A worker who finds an unlabeled container should not open it or try to identify it by smell. Instead, set it aside and report it to the supervisor, who will arrange for proper identification or disposal.
items.stem: According to the passage, what does the signal word on a chemical label tell the reader?
choices: The type of hazard the chemical presents
The name of the company that made the product
The date the container was filled
How serious the hazard is
items.explanation: The passage says a signal word tells the reader how serious the hazard is, and it gives Danger for the more severe hazards and Warning for the less severe ones. The type of hazard is shown by the pictograms, and the manufacturer and date are never mentioned.

items.passage: A steel ship floats even though a solid bar of steel sinks. The reason is that an object immersed in water is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. A solid bar displaces only a small volume of water, far less than its own weight, so it sinks. A ship's hull, by contrast, encloses a large volume of air. The hull pushes aside a great deal of water, and once the weight of that displaced water equals the weight of the ship and everything aboard, the ship stops sinking and floats. Loading more cargo makes the vessel sit lower, displacing more water until balance is restored again. If the hull is breached and water replaces the air inside, the ship loses that advantage.
items.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a ship sinks when its hull floods because
choices: water inside the hull adds weight without pushing aside any additional water
the cargo shifts to one side of the vessel
steel becomes heavier when it is wet
the upward force of the water disappears completely
items.explanation: The passage explains that a ship floats because its air-filled hull displaces water equal to its weight, and the last sentence says that when water replaces the air inside, the ship loses that advantage. Water inside the hull makes the ship heavier but does not increase the water pushed aside, so the upward force can no longer match the weight. The upward force does not vanish, steel does not change weight, and cargo shifting is never mentioned.

items.passage: Fatigue is a safety hazard that does not announce itself. A crew member who has been awake for twenty hours may feel alert yet react as slowly as someone who has been drinking. For this reason, watch schedules on vessels are built around rest as well as duty. Supervisors are expected to track hours, not just assign them, and to rotate assignments so that no one stands the most demanding watch night after night. Crew members have a duty too: they should report when they are too tired to work safely, even if that means a colleague has to cover. Caffeine and cold air can mask drowsiness for a short time, but they do not restore judgment. Only sleep does.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Caffeine is an acceptable substitute for sleep on long watches
Night watches should be eliminated aboard vessels
Because fatigue impairs people without their noticing, both supervisors and crew must actively manage rest
Supervisors alone are responsible for preventing fatigue among the crew
items.explanation: The first sentence says fatigue does not announce itself, and the body of the passage assigns duties to supervisors, who must track and rotate hours, and to crew members, who must report when they are too tired. Choice A is contradicted by the statement that caffeine does not restore judgment, choice B is never suggested, and choice D ignores the sentence that says crew members have a duty too.

items.stem: As used in the passage, the word mask most nearly means
choices: protect the face from injury
hide or cover up
celebrate with costumes
measure with precision
items.explanation: The passage says caffeine and cold air can mask drowsiness for a short time but do not restore judgment, so mask means to hide the drowsiness without removing it. The other choices do not fit a sentence about drowsiness.

items.passage: The sinking of the passenger liner Titanic in April 1912, after it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic, led to an international response. Maritime nations met in London the following year and agreed on new rules for the safety of life at sea, including requirements for lifeboats and continuous radio watches. They also agreed to fund a patrol that would locate icebergs drifting south into shipping lanes and broadcast their positions. The United States was asked to run it, and the duty went to the Revenue Cutter Service, which later became the Coast Guard. The International Ice Patrol began operating in 1914. Its methods have shifted from cutters to aircraft to satellite data, but its purpose, keeping ships informed of ice hazards, has stayed the same.
items.stem: According to the passage, the International Ice Patrol was created in order to
choices: rescue survivors of the Titanic
locate icebergs in shipping lanes and broadcast their positions
build lifeboats for passenger liners
test new types of radio equipment
items.explanation: The passage says the nations agreed to fund a patrol that would locate icebergs drifting south into shipping lanes and broadcast their positions, and the last sentence repeats that its purpose is keeping ships informed of ice hazards. Lifeboats and radio watches were separate rules, and the patrol began in 1914, two years after the Titanic sank.

items.passage: Portable fire extinguishers are meant for small fires that have just started. Before using one, make sure everyone else has been alerted and that you have a clear exit behind you. Then follow four steps. Pull the pin that locks the handle. Aim the nozzle at the base of the flames, not at the smoke or the top of the fire, since the fuel is at the bottom. Squeeze the handle to release the agent. Sweep the nozzle from side to side across the base until the fire is out, then watch for any sign that it is rekindling. If the fire grows, if the room fills with smoke, or if the extinguisher empties before the flames are out, leave at once and close the door behind you.
items.stem: Which of the following lists the four extinguisher steps in the order the passage gives them?
choices: Aim, pull, squeeze, sweep
Pull, squeeze, aim, sweep
Sweep, aim, pull, squeeze
Pull, aim, squeeze, sweep
items.explanation: The passage says to pull the pin, aim the nozzle at the base of the flames, squeeze the handle, and sweep from side to side, in that order. Each of the other choices moves at least one step out of place.

items.passage: A satellite navigation receiver does not send any signal of its own. Instead it listens for timing signals broadcast by a group of satellites orbiting the Earth. Each signal carries the exact time it left the satellite and the satellite's position. Because radio waves travel at a known speed, the receiver can calculate how far away each satellite is by measuring how long its signal took to arrive. Knowing the distance to one satellite places the receiver somewhere on a huge sphere. Distances to three satellites narrow the position to a point, and a fourth satellite corrects for errors in the receiver's inexpensive clock. The result is a fix accurate to within a few meters, available anywhere on Earth with a clear view of the sky.
items.stem: According to the passage, why does a receiver need a signal from a fourth satellite?
choices: To correct for errors in the receiver's inexpensive clock
To send its own position back to the ground
To boost the strength of the other three signals
To replace a satellite that has stopped working
items.explanation: The passage states that distances to three satellites narrow the position to a point and a fourth satellite corrects for errors in the receiver's inexpensive clock. The first sentence says the receiver sends no signal of its own, which rules out choice B, and the passage says nothing about boosting signals or replacing satellites.

Each signal carries the exact time it left the satellite and the satellite's position. items.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
choices: A History of Space Exploration
Why Navigation Receivers Need Expensive Clocks
How a Receiver Finds Its Position From Satellite Signals
The Speed of Radio Waves
items.explanation: The passage follows one idea from start to finish: a receiver measures signal travel time to find distances to satellites and combines them into a position. Choice A is far broader than the passage, choice B contradicts the statement that the receiver's clock is inexpensive, and choice D is one supporting detail rather than the subject.

items.passage: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are related conditions, but they call for different responses. Heat exhaustion develops when the body loses more fluid and salt than it takes in. The person sweats heavily, feels weak or dizzy, and may have a headache or cramps. Moving to shade, loosening clothing, and sipping cool water will usually bring recovery within an hour. Heat stroke is a medical emergency. The body's cooling system has failed, the skin may be hot and dry rather than sweaty, and the person may be confused or lose consciousness. Call for emergency help at once and cool the person aggressively with water and moving air while waiting. Never give fluids to someone who is confused or not fully awake, because they may choke.
items.stem: Based on the passage, a worker in hot weather who has stopped sweating and is confused is most likely
choices: recovering from heat exhaustion
simply tired and should rest in the shade
in need of a large drink of cool water
suffering from heat stroke and in need of emergency help
items.explanation: The passage describes heat stroke as the condition in which the skin may be hot and dry rather than sweaty and the person may be confused, and it calls heat stroke a medical emergency. Heavy sweating belongs to heat exhaustion, so choice A does not fit, and the last sentence warns never to give fluids to someone who is confused, which rules out choice C.

items.passage: Rip currents are narrow channels of fast-moving water that flow away from the beach and out past the breaking waves. They form when water pushed ashore by waves finds a low spot in a sandbar and drains back to sea through it. A rip current does not pull a swimmer under, but it can carry even a strong swimmer offshore faster than the swimmer can fight back. People drown when they exhaust themselves trying to swim straight toward the beach against the flow. The recommended escape is to stay calm, float, and swim parallel to the shoreline until the pull weakens, then angle back toward land. Rip currents are often visible as a gap in the line of breaking waves or a streak of choppy, discolored water.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Rip currents drag swimmers beneath the surface of the water
Rip currents carry swimmers offshore, and the way to escape is to swim parallel to the beach rather than straight in
Only weak swimmers are at risk from rip currents
Sandbars should be removed from public beaches
items.explanation: The passage explains what a rip current does, that it carries swimmers out past the waves, and then gives the recommended escape of swimming parallel to the shoreline. Choice A is contradicted by the sentence that says a rip current does not pull a swimmer under, choice C is contradicted by the mention of strong swimmers, and choice D is never suggested.

items.passage: Tanks, voids, and other confined spaces aboard a vessel can hold air that is unsafe to breathe even when nothing looks wrong. Rust forming on steel consumes oxygen, and fuel residue or decaying material can release gases that are invisible and may have no odor. No one may enter such a space until a qualified person has tested the atmosphere with a calibrated meter and recorded the readings on an entry permit. An attendant must remain outside the opening for the entire time anyone is inside, keeping in contact and ready to call for rescue. The attendant never enters to attempt a rescue alone; most deaths in confined spaces are would-be rescuers who were overcome by the same atmosphere.
items.stem: According to the passage, who tests the atmosphere of a confined space before anyone enters?
choices: The attendant stationed outside the opening
The person who is about to enter the space
A qualified person using a calibrated meter
The vessel's commanding officer
items.explanation: The passage says no one may enter until a qualified person has tested the atmosphere with a calibrated meter and recorded the readings on an entry permit. The attendant's job is to remain outside and keep in contact, and the passage does not assign the test to the entrant or the commanding officer.

items.passage: Tanks, voids, and other confined spaces aboard a vessel can hold air that is unsafe to breathe even when nothing looks wrong. Rust forming on steel consumes oxygen, and fuel residue or decaying material can release gases that are invisible and may have no odor. No one may enter such a space until a qualified person has tested the atmosphere with a calibrated meter and recorded the readings on an entry permit. An attendant must remain outside the opening for the entire time anyone is inside, keeping in contact and ready to call for rescue. The attendant never enters to attempt a rescue alone; most deaths in confined spaces are would-be rescuers who were overcome by the same atmosphere.
items.stem: The author most likely includes the final sentence about would-be rescuers in order to
choices: explain why the attendant must not enter the space to attempt a rescue alone
describe the history of confined space accidents aboard ships
argue that an attendant is not really necessary
show that confined spaces are rarely dangerous
items.explanation: The sentence directly follows the rule that the attendant never enters to attempt a rescue alone, and it gives the reason: most deaths in confined spaces are would-be rescuers overcome by the same atmosphere. It supports the rule rather than questioning it, and it makes the spaces sound more dangerous, not less.

items.passage: Saltwater is hard on metal, and boats that live in it fight a constant battle against corrosion. The most familiar form is rust, but a less obvious form occurs when two different metals touch each other in seawater. The water acts as a conductor, a weak electric current flows between the metals, and the less noble of the two gradually dissolves. Boat builders counter this by bolting blocks of zinc to the hull near the propeller and shaft. Zinc is less noble than steel or bronze, so the current attacks the zinc instead of the expensive parts it protects. These blocks are called sacrificial anodes. They are meant to waste away and must be inspected regularly and replaced before they are gone.
items.stem: As used in the passage, the word sacrificial most nearly means
choices: connected to a religious ceremony
given up in order to protect something else
extremely expensive to replace
permanently attached to the hull
items.explanation: The passage says the current attacks the zinc instead of the expensive parts it protects and that the blocks are meant to waste away. The zinc is given up so that other parts survive, which is what sacrificial means here. Choice D is contradicted by the statement that the blocks must be replaced, and the passage never calls them expensive.

items.passage: Most serious accidents are preceded by near misses, moments when something went wrong but no one happened to be hurt. A dropped wrench that lands next to a foot rather than on it is still a dropped wrench. Organizations that treat these events as free lessons tend to have fewer injuries, because the conditions that caused the near miss get fixed before they cause harm. That only works if people report them, and people report them only when they trust that doing so will not get them or their coworkers in trouble. This command therefore asks every member to report near misses through the anonymous form in the shop office. The goal is to learn what almost happened, not to assign blame.
items.stem: The author's main purpose in this passage is to
choices: announce a new penalty for dropping tools in the shop
explain the safe way to handle a wrench
describe a recent accident in detail
encourage members to report near misses by explaining their value and promising no blame
items.explanation: The passage explains that near misses are free lessons, notes that people report them only when they trust they will not get in trouble, and then asks every member to use the anonymous form. The final sentence states the goal is to learn, not to assign blame. The dropped wrench is only an example, and no accident or penalty is described.

items.passage: When a vessel ties up to a pier, several lines share the work of holding it in place. Bow and stern lines run from the ends of the vessel to the pier at an angle and keep the hull from drifting away. Spring lines run nearly parallel to the pier, one leading aft from a point near the bow and one leading forward from a point near the stern, and they stop the vessel from sliding ahead or astern along the pier. Breast lines run straight across from the hull to the pier and hold it snug against the fenders. A vessel that is surging fore and aft at its berth usually needs its spring lines adjusted, while one that is drifting away from the pier needs attention to the breast lines.
items.stem: According to the passage, which lines keep a vessel from sliding forward or backward along the pier?
choices: Spring lines
Bow and stern lines
Breast lines
Fender lines
items.explanation: The passage says spring lines run nearly parallel to the pier and stop the vessel from sliding ahead or astern. Bow and stern lines keep the hull from drifting away, breast lines hold it snug against the fenders, and fender lines are not mentioned in the passage at all.

items.passage: A small craft advisory is issued when sustained winds or seas are expected to reach levels that can be hazardous to smaller vessels. The advisory does not define what counts as a small craft. That judgment is left to the operator, because a vessel's ability to handle rough water depends on its design, its loading, and the experience of the people aboard as much as on its length. A heavily loaded open boat with an inexperienced crew may be in danger in conditions that a smaller but well-built boat with a seasoned skipper handles routinely. Operators who hear the advisory are expected to compare the forecast with their own vessel and crew honestly, rather than assuming that the warning applies only to boats smaller than theirs.
items.stem: The passage suggests that the operator of a large but heavily loaded boat with an inexperienced crew should
choices: ignore the advisory because the boat is not a small craft
wait for an official definition of small craft before deciding
treat the advisory as applying to their own vessel and crew
assume the advisory is meant only for open boats
items.explanation: The passage says the ability to handle rough water depends on design, loading, and experience as much as on length, and it gives the example of a heavily loaded boat with an inexperienced crew being in danger. The last sentence tells operators to compare the forecast with their own vessel and crew honestly rather than assuming the warning applies only to smaller boats, which rules out choices A and D. The passage says the definition is deliberately left to the operator, so choice B is wrong.

items.passage: A magnetic compass does not point to the geographic North Pole. It aligns with Earth's magnetic field, whose northern pole lies hundreds of miles from the geographic pole and drifts slowly from year to year. The angle between true north and magnetic north at a given place is called variation, and it differs from one part of the world to another. In some regions it is only a degree or two; in others it exceeds twenty degrees. Nautical charts print the local variation inside the compass rose along with the annual rate of change. A navigator who plots a course on the chart in true degrees must convert it to magnetic degrees before steering by the compass, or the vessel will slowly wander off its intended track.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Earth's magnetic pole never changes its position
Nautical charts are more reliable than magnetic compasses
A compass points to magnetic north, so navigators must correct for variation when steering a charted course
Variation is about twenty degrees everywhere in the world
items.explanation: The passage opens by saying a compass does not point to the geographic pole, defines variation, and ends by saying a navigator must convert true degrees to magnetic degrees or wander off track. Choice A is contradicted by the statement that the pole drifts, choice D is contradicted by the sentence that variation differs by region, and choice B compares two tools in a way the passage never does.

items.passage: On a flight line, a loose tool is more than a nuisance. A wrench left inside an engine cowling or a screw dropped on the ramp can be pulled into a jet intake or jam a control surface. For this reason aviation maintenance units practice strict tool control. Each toolbox has a shadowed cutout for every item, so a missing tool is obvious at a glance. Tools are counted out at the start of a job and counted back in at the end, and the count is recorded. If anything is unaccounted for, the aircraft does not fly until the item is found or the area has been searched and cleared by a supervisor. The system is slow and sometimes frustrating, but it is far cheaper than losing an aircraft.
items.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Strict tool accountability on the flight line prevents loose items from damaging aircraft
Shadowed toolboxes are too costly for most maintenance units
Every aircraft should be searched after each flight
Supervisors are responsible for counting tools in and out
items.explanation: The passage begins with the danger of a loose tool, describes the tool control system of shadowed boxes and counts, and closes by saying the system is far cheaper than losing an aircraft. Choice B is never stated, choice C goes beyond the passage, and choice D is wrong because supervisors are mentioned only for clearing a searched area, not for counting.

items.passage: Fog is simply a cloud that forms at ground level. It appears when air is cooled to the point where it can no longer hold all of its water vapor, and the excess condenses into tiny droplets. Along a coast the most common type is advection fog, which forms when warm, moist air drifts over a cooler sea surface. Because the ocean changes temperature slowly, this kind of fog can persist for days and advance and retreat with the wind. Radiation fog, by contrast, forms over land on clear, calm nights when the ground loses heat to the sky and chills the air just above it; it usually burns off within a few hours of sunrise. Mariners treat fog as a serious hazard because it hides other vessels, buoys, and the shoreline itself.
items.stem: As used in the passage, the word persist most nearly means
choices: disappear quickly
grow thicker
rise into the sky
continue or last
items.explanation: The passage says this kind of fog can persist for days because the ocean changes temperature slowly, contrasting it with radiation fog that burns off within hours. So persist means to keep going for a long time. Choice A is the opposite, and choices C and B describe changes the passage does not mention.

items.passage: If a piece of equipment fails intermittently, working one moment and dead the next, report the behavior exactly as you observed it rather than guessing at the cause. Note what the equipment was doing when the fault appeared, how long it lasted, and whether anything such as vibration, heat, or a nearby motor starting seemed to trigger it. Intermittent faults are among the hardest for technicians to track down, because the problem may not show itself while the equipment is on the bench. A clear description of the conditions under which the failure occurred lets the technician reproduce it. A vague report such as 'it stopped working' may send the technician down the wrong path and leave the real fault in place.
items.stem: As used in the passage, the word intermittently most nearly means
choices: permanently
at irregular intervals, stopping and starting
very loudly
for the very first time
items.explanation: The passage defines the word right after using it: working one moment and dead the next. Equipment that behaves this way stops and starts, which is what intermittently means. A permanent failure would show itself on the bench, which the passage says intermittent faults may not do.

items.passage: In the nineteenth century, some shipowners deliberately overloaded old vessels and insured them heavily, knowing that if the ship sank the insurance would pay more than the ship was worth. Sailors called them coffin ships. A British member of Parliament, Samuel Plimsoll, campaigned for years against the practice, and in 1876 a law required merchant ships to carry a mark on the hull showing the deepest level to which they could legally be loaded. If the mark disappeared under the water, the ship was overloaded and could be held in port. The symbol, a circle with a horizontal line through it, is still painted on the sides of cargo ships around the world and is widely known as the Plimsoll line.
items.stem: The passage implies that before 1876, overloading an old ship
choices: was illegal but rarely punished
was practiced mainly on newly built vessels
was impossible for inspectors to detect
could be profitable for the owner even if the ship was lost
items.explanation: The first sentence says owners overloaded old vessels and insured them heavily, knowing that if the ship sank the insurance would pay more than the ship was worth. That means a loss could still bring a profit. The passage says a law was needed in 1876, which suggests the practice was not already illegal, and it specifies old vessels, not new ones.

items.passage: Checklists exist because memory is unreliable, especially when a task is routine. A pilot who has run the same pre-flight checks a thousand times is exactly the person most likely to skip one, not because of carelessness but because the mind fills in the familiar pattern and reports it done. Reading each item aloud and physically touching the switch or gauge it names interrupts that pattern. Crews sometimes complain that the practice feels childish or slows them down. It does slow them down, by a minute or two. Against that cost stands the record of accidents in which a skilled, experienced crew missed a single step they had performed correctly on every previous flight. The checklist is not a sign of distrust. It is a tool for the kind of error that skill alone cannot prevent.
items.stem: The author's main purpose in this passage is to
choices: describe the steps of a pre-flight inspection
persuade readers that careful use of checklists is worthwhile even for experienced crews
criticize pilots for being careless during routine tasks
explain how memory develops in young children
items.explanation: The passage acknowledges the complaint that checklists feel childish and slow, then answers it with the record of accidents in which skilled crews missed one step, and ends by calling the checklist a tool for errors that skill alone cannot prevent. That structure is an argument, not a description. The author specifically says skipped steps are not because of carelessness, so choice C is contradicted.

items.passage: A hurricane is powered by warm ocean water. When sea surface temperatures rise above roughly 80 degrees Fahrenheit, large amounts of water evaporate into the air above. As that moist air rises and cools, the vapor condenses into clouds and releases the heat it absorbed during evaporation. The released heat warms the surrounding air, which rises faster and draws in more moist air from the surface. Earth's rotation sets the inflowing air spinning, and a storm with an organized circulation can grow as long as it remains over warm water. When a hurricane crosses onto land or drifts over cooler water, its fuel supply is cut off and it begins to weaken, though it can still produce dangerous rain and flooding far inland.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
choices: A History of Atlantic Storms
Why Hurricanes Never Reach Land
Where Hurricanes Get Their Energy
How to Prepare for Coastal Flooding
items.explanation: The first sentence states that a hurricane is powered by warm ocean water, and every following sentence explains how that energy is released and why the storm weakens when the warm water is gone. Choice B is contradicted by the statement that hurricanes cross onto land, and choices A and D cover topics the passage does not discuss.

items.passage: A watch turnover is the handoff between the person leaving a post and the person taking it over, and the quality of that handoff matters. The oncoming watchstander should arrive early enough to read the log and ask questions before assuming responsibility. The offgoing watchstander should cover the current status of all equipment, anything unusual that happened during the watch, any orders received from the officer in charge, and any tasks that are still in progress. Both should walk the space together and look at the gauges and alarms rather than describing them from memory. The turnover is complete only when the oncoming person states clearly that they have the watch and the log records the time. A rushed or casual turnover is a common root cause of incidents.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
choices: Conducting a Proper Watch Turnover
A History of Shipboard Watches
Why Alarm Systems Fail
How to Read an Equipment Log
items.explanation: The passage defines a watch turnover in its first sentence and then lists what each watchstander should do and when the turnover is complete. Reading the log is only one step, so choice D is too narrow, and the passage says nothing about history or about alarm failures.
